Savour
SAV-ur
n. and v. (rendering Hebrew rēach, Greek osmē/euodia)
From French saveur, Latin sapor, taste or flavour, from sapere, to taste and also to be wise — the Latin joins discernment and flavour in one verb. In the Authorized Version savour usually renders the Hebrew rēach, a smell, especially the smell of a sacrifice ascending, and Greek osmē, an odour.

Biblical Definition

A savour in Scripture is chiefly a smell that rises, and it is the standing figure for a sacrifice God accepts. After the flood, the first recorded worship of the new world is met this way: “And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake” (Genesis 8:21) — not that God has nostrils, but that the offering pleased Him and secured a promise. The New Testament identifies what all those altars were pointing at: “Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour” (Ephesians 5:2). The figure then extends to the church's witness, and with a terrible double edge: “we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish” (2 Corinthians 2:15) — the same gospel, the same preachers, and two opposite outcomes, so that faithfulness cannot be measured by reception. And the word is used of a quality that can be lost: “if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” (Matthew 5:13). Savour is thus what a thing gives off — the sacrifice its smoke, the Christian his life, the salt its bite — and Scripture is concerned throughout with whether it rises to God or has gone flat.

Webster 1828 Definition

Taste or odour; that which a thing gives off; in Scripture, the sweet savour of a sacrifice ascending to God, Christ's offering of Himself as a sweetsmelling savour, believers as a savour of Christ to the saved and the perishing, and salt that has lost its savour.

SAVOUR, n. 1. Taste or odour; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste or smell.

2. Scent; odour; as, a sweet savour.

3. Character or quality perceived; as, doctrine that has a savour of truth.

4. From French saveur, Latin sapor, from sapere, to taste, also to be wise.

5. In Scripture, the LORD smelled a sweet savour, Gen. 8; a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour, Eph. 5.

Key Scripture

Genesis 8:21 — "And the LORD smelled a sweet savour; and the LORD said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake; for the imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth; neither will I again smite any more every thing living, as I have done. a"

Ephesians 5:2 — "And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour."

2 Corinthians 2:15 — "For we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish:"

Matthew 5:13 — "Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men."

Modern Corruption

The sweet savour is read as though God were appeased by the ritual itself, or else the whole sacrificial vocabulary is dismissed as primitive; and ministry is judged by how agreeable its savour proves to those who receive it.

expand to see more

Two opposite misreadings of the sweet savour persist. The first is the pagan one Israel kept falling into, in which the smoke itself placates the deity, so that sacrifice becomes a transaction and the worshipper's heart is irrelevant. The prophets demolish this without qualification: God will not eat the flesh of bulls, He delights not in the blood of goats, and the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. The second is the modern dismissal, which reads the whole altar system as a primitive stage the faith outgrew, and then finds the doctrine of the atonement embarrassing for the same reason. But Ephesians 5:2 will not let the sacrificial category go: the death of Christ is presented as an offering and a sacrifice to God, offered by Him, received by the Father, and pleasing to Him. Take away the altar and the cross becomes an accident or a demonstration rather than a propitiation.

The second corruption is nearer to home. 2 Corinthians 2:15-16 says that faithful ministry smells of life to some and of death to others, and that the difference lies in the hearers, not in the savour. Modern ministry is routinely evaluated by the opposite rule: the measure of a message is how it lands, and a savour that offends is taken as proof that something went wrong. Paul says the reverse can be true, and asks “who is sufficient for these things?” The principle to recover is that the church's business is to be a sweet savour of Christ — faithful in doctrine and holy in life — and to leave the two outcomes with God. Salt that has lost its savour is not salt that has offended nobody; it is salt that has become indistinguishable from the meat it was meant to preserve.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rēach, a smell or odour, especially of sacrifice; nīchoach, soothing or restful, the sweet savour of acceptance; Greek osmē, odour, and euodia, a fragrance.

expand to see more

Hebrew rēach (H7381) — a smell or odour; the standing word for the savour of an offering ascending.

Hebrew nīchoach (H5207) — soothing, restful; joined to rēach to mean a savour of rest or acceptance (Leviticus 1:9).

Greek osmē (G3744) — an odour or smell; used of the ointment that filled the house (John 12:3) and of the savour of Christ.

Greek euodia (G2175) — a sweet smell, fragrance; “a sweetsmelling savour” (Ephesians 5:2; Philippians 4:18).

Greek mōrainō (G3471) — to make foolish or insipid; the verb behind salt that has lost its savour (Matthew 5:13).

Usage

"Of a sacrifice accepted: the LORD smelled a sweet savour (Genesis 8:21)."

"Of the atonement offered to God: a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour (Ephesians 5:2)."

"Of ministry with two outcomes: a sweet savour of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish (2 Corinthians 2:15)."
